prompt.context_jp: 東京第一銀行中野支店の営業を終えた午後、花咲舞___副支店長席の前に立ち、真っすぐに相馬健を見据えていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 花咲舞___副支店長席の前に立ち、真っすぐに相馬健を見据えていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that introduces Mai as the ongoing topic of this opening scene.

feedback.correct_en: This is the opening of the chapter and Mai is being set up as the topic whose actions we will follow. は frames her as the theme of the narrative that follows.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would mark her as newly spotted information answering 'who is standing there?', but the narrator is anchoring her as the protagonist, not announcing her presence.

contrast_examples.jp: 花咲舞は銀行員だ。
contrast_examples.en: Mai is a bank employee. (topic statement)

contrast_examples.jp: あっ、花咲舞が来た！
contrast_examples.en: Oh, Mai came! (newly observed)

prompt.context_jp: 相馬が舞の提案を押し返す場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 銀行には守るべき慣例というもの___あるんだ。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits this existential assertion Souma uses to shut Mai down?

feedback.correct_en: Souma is asserting the existence of something (customs) as new information to counter Mai. ある-type existential clauses with an indefinite subject take が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would turn 'customs' into a known topic, as if they'd already been discussing it. Here he's introducing the concept into the argument.

contrast_examples.jp: ここに本がある。
contrast_examples.en: There is a book here.

contrast_examples.jp: その本は机の上にある。
contrast_examples.en: That (already-known) book is on the desk.

prompt.context_jp: 若手行員たちが盛り上がる会場で、ひとり相馬だけが浮かない表情をしている。
prompt.prompt_jp: 相馬___片隅の椅子で、まだこれが夢であってほしいと願うような顔をしている。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle highlights Souma against the celebrating crowd?

feedback.correct_en: Everyone else is enjoying the party; は picks out Souma contrastively — as for Souma (unlike the others), he looks miserable.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would read as identifying who among a set is making that face, but the discourse is contrasting Souma's mood with the room's cheer.

contrast_examples.jp: みんなは笑っているが、彼は黙っている。
contrast_examples.en: Everyone is laughing, but he is silent. (contrastive は)

contrast_examples.jp: 誰が黙っているの？ — 彼が黙っている。
contrast_examples.en: Who's silent? — He is. (identifying が)

prompt.context_jp: 会場の全員がくつろいでいる中で――
prompt.prompt_jp: 相馬だけ___、グラスの氷を意味もなくかき混ぜていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle goes with 「〜だけ」 to pick Souma out as the sole exception?

feedback.correct_en: 「〜だけが」 exhaustively identifies the one and only person doing something — only Souma, nobody else. が is the natural partner of だけ in this exclusive sense.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「だけは」 would mean 'at least Souma / Souma above all,' giving a very different, emphatic nuance that doesn't match the quiet exclusion here.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼だけが知っている。
contrast_examples.en: Only he knows (nobody else).

contrast_examples.jp: 彼だけは知っている。
contrast_examples.en: He at least knows (emphatic, often contrastive).

prompt.context_jp: 田中が相馬に本部異動の知らせを届ける場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 喜べ、君に内示___出た。来月から本部だぞ。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle announces this fresh news to Souma?

feedback.correct_en: The 内示 is brand-new information being delivered — 'an informal notice has come out (for you).' New-info subjects of 出る take が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would presuppose that the 内示 was already a known topic, which contradicts the surprise/announcement framing of 「喜べ」.

contrast_examples.jp: 結果が出た！
contrast_examples.en: The results are out! (announcement)

contrast_examples.jp: 結果はまだ出ていない。
contrast_examples.en: The results (as for them) aren't out yet. (known topic)

prompt.context_jp: 内示を聞いた相馬の心境。
prompt.prompt_jp: 相馬の胸の中で長く凍りついていた何か___、一気に解けていった。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks this 'something' that suddenly melts?

feedback.correct_en: 「何か」 (something) is an indefinite, newly-introduced subject — exactly the environment where が is required.
feedback.incorrect_en: Indefinite 「何か」 almost never takes は, because は presupposes a known/identifiable topic, and 「何か」 is by definition not identified.

contrast_examples.jp: 何かが聞こえる。
contrast_examples.en: I can hear something.

contrast_examples.jp: その音は聞こえない。
contrast_examples.en: I can't hear that (known) sound.

prompt.context_jp: 本部で三か月ひとりで働いた相馬に、辛島が告げる。
prompt.prompt_jp: ようやく部下___決まったと辛島から告げられた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks 'subordinate' in this announcement?

feedback.correct_en: The subordinate is new information finally popping into existence after a long wait — 「ようやく〜が決まった」 is the natural new-event pattern.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would require the 部下 to be an already-established topic, but this sentence is announcing that a subordinate has materialized at last.

contrast_examples.jp: やっと答えが見つかった。
contrast_examples.en: I finally found the answer (new result).

contrast_examples.jp: その答えはもう知っている。
contrast_examples.en: I already know that (known) answer.

prompt.context_jp: 辛島の部屋のドアの向こうから――
prompt.prompt_jp: 扉の向こうから若い女性の声___控えめに答え、続いてノブがゆっくりと回された。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits this sudden sound from behind the door?

feedback.correct_en: A voice newly appearing in the scene is prototypical new-information が — the reader hears it along with Souma for the first time.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame 'the young woman's voice' as a pre-established topic, breaking the surprise of the moment.

contrast_examples.jp: どこかで声がした。
contrast_examples.en: A voice came from somewhere (new perception).

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女の声はよく通る。
contrast_examples.en: Her voice carries well (describing a known topic).

prompt.context_jp: ドアを開けた舞の顔を見た瞬間――
prompt.prompt_jp: 現れた顔を見た瞬間、相馬の全身___硬直する。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits this unexpected bodily reaction?

feedback.correct_en: This is a sudden, event-report sentence: Souma's whole body freezes at that instant. Event descriptions of involuntary reactions take が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make it a general topic-comment ('as for Souma's body, it freezes'), losing the surprise and immediacy of the moment.

contrast_examples.jp: 急に体が震えた。
contrast_examples.en: My body suddenly trembled (event).

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の体は丈夫だ。
contrast_examples.en: His body is strong (general property).

prompt.context_jp: 廊下の先から真藤常務が現れ、周囲が姿勢を正す。
prompt.prompt_jp: 紺のスーツを隙なく着こなしたその男___、部下を従えて悠然と歩いていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle introduces this man as the focal topic of the sentence?

feedback.correct_en: The previous sentences have already established that a man is approaching; this line now zooms in on him as the topic and describes him. は presents him as given and comments on him.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would re-introduce him as fresh information, but the narration has already pointed the reader at him — we're elaborating, not announcing.

contrast_examples.jp: その男は静かに歩いていた。
contrast_examples.en: The man (we know of) was walking calmly.

contrast_examples.jp: 一人の男が歩いてきた。
contrast_examples.en: A (new) man came walking.

prompt.context_jp: 真藤が頭取候補だと相馬から告げられて――
prompt.prompt_jp: 頭取候補という肩書きの重み___、舞の胸にじわりと沈んでいく。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks this weight that sinks into Mai's chest?

feedback.correct_en: The 'weight of the title' is a newly-felt sensation emerging in Mai in this moment — a prototypical event with が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would turn this specific felt impact into a general topic, flattening the in-the-moment narration.

contrast_examples.jp: 不安が胸に広がった。
contrast_examples.en: Anxiety spread through her chest (event).

contrast_examples.jp: 不安はいつも彼女を襲う。
contrast_examples.en: Anxiety (as a topic) always strikes her.

prompt.context_jp: 向島支店を出た帰り道、舞が隣の相馬の表情に気づく。
prompt.prompt_jp: 隣を歩く相馬の横顔には、慣れた者だけが浮かべる諦めの色___あった。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks the 'look of resignation' that was there on his profile?

feedback.correct_en: This is an existential 「〜がある」 clause introducing something Mai newly notices on Souma's face. Indefinite 'a shade of resignation' takes が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would require 「諦めの色」 to be a known topic, but the whole point is that Mai is just now spotting it there.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の目に涙があった。
contrast_examples.en: There were tears in his eyes.

contrast_examples.jp: その涙は乾いていた。
contrast_examples.en: Those (known) tears had dried.

prompt.context_jp: 矢島が「たかが窓口の仕事」と口にした瞬間――
prompt.prompt_jp: 舞の顔つき___微かに変わったのを、相馬は横目で捉えていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks Mai's expression inside this subordinate (のを) clause?

feedback.correct_en: Inside a subordinate 「〜のを」 clause describing a one-off event the subject takes が, not は. は is generally blocked inside such embedded event clauses.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would be strange here because the clause is naming a specific momentary change that Souma observes, not stating a general fact about Mai's face.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が笑うのを見た。
contrast_examples.en: I saw him smile.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は笑うのが好きだ。
contrast_examples.en: He (topic) likes to smile.

prompt.context_jp: 混み合う茅場町支店の窓口で――
prompt.prompt_jp: 窓口では中島だけ___、慣れた手つきで次々と伝票を捌いていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle pairs with 「だけ」 to spotlight Nakajima as the only competent one?

feedback.correct_en: 「〜だけが」 exclusively identifies Nakajima among all the tellers: she is the one and only person handling things smoothly. が delivers the exhaustive-listing reading.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「だけは」 would shift to 'at least Nakajima' with a defensive/concessive flavor — not the pure 'only her, nobody else' observation the scene wants.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女だけが仕事ができる。
contrast_examples.en: Only she can do the job (exclusive).

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女だけは諦めなかった。
contrast_examples.en: She alone didn't give up (emphatic/contrastive).

prompt.context_jp: 翌朝の支店。昨夜の件を引きずる相馬――
prompt.prompt_jp: 相馬___椅子に沈み込むように腰を下ろし、山と積まれた伝票の束を憎らしげに睨みつける。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle re-establishes Souma as the topic of this new paragraph?

feedback.correct_en: A new scene opens and the camera settles on Souma as the paragraph's topic for a stretch of description. は signals 'about Souma' and licenses the chain of verbs that follow.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would read as newly spotting him in the scene, but the reader already knows who he is — we're resuming narration about him.

contrast_examples.jp: 翌朝、彼は机に向かった。
contrast_examples.en: The next morning, he sat down at his desk. (topic resumption)

contrast_examples.jp: そのとき彼が入ってきた。
contrast_examples.en: At that moment he came in. (new event)

prompt.context_jp: ようやく部下が決まったと聞かされた直後。
prompt.prompt_jp: 優秀な若い女子行員___来ると聞き、相馬は素直に胸を撫でおろした。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks this incoming new employee?

feedback.correct_en: Inside a 「〜と聞き」 content clause reporting a fresh piece of information, an indefinite subject like '優秀な若い女子行員' takes が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would presuppose that this particular woman was already a known topic — but Souma has only just heard she's coming, with no identity attached.

contrast_examples.jp: 新人が来ると聞いた。
contrast_examples.en: I heard a new hire is coming.

contrast_examples.jp: その新人はまだ来ていない。
contrast_examples.en: That (known) new hire hasn't come yet.

prompt.context_jp: 舞が忘年会の提案を繰り返している場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 今年の忘年会を若手主導のパーティーに変えるという舞の提案を、相馬___さっきから受け流し続けている。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle keeps Souma as the ongoing topic in contrast to Mai's proposal?

feedback.correct_en: The sentence sets Mai's proposal first, then switches the topic to Souma to describe his stance toward it. は carries that topic shift and comment nicely.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would news-report Souma into the scene as if the reader didn't know him, but he was already introduced in the previous sentence.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女の案を、彼はいつも無視する。
contrast_examples.en: Her ideas — he always ignores them. (topic/contrast)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女の案に、彼が反対した。
contrast_examples.en: He opposed her idea. (reporting a new event)

prompt.context_jp: 何度も同じ答えを返される舞の心境。
prompt.prompt_jp: 同じやり取りを何度も繰り返す上司の態度に、舞はいい加減___し始めていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which word captures Mai's growing fed-up feeling?

feedback.correct_en: 「うんざりする」 = to be fed up / sick of it. 「いい加減うんざり」 is a very common collocation meaning 'about to lose patience.'
feedback.incorrect_en: 「うっかり」 is 'careless/absent-minded,' and 「びっくり」 is 'startled' — neither matches the slow-boil annoyance of hearing the same answer again and again.

contrast_examples.jp: 同じ話にはもううんざりだ。
contrast_examples.en: I'm fed up with the same story.

contrast_examples.jp: うっかり約束を忘れた。
contrast_examples.en: I carelessly forgot the appointment.

prompt.context_jp: 舞が「慣例」を言い換えて相馬に反論する。
prompt.prompt_jp: それは慣例ではなくて、ただの___ですよね？
prompt.prompt_en: Which word does Mai use to accuse the custom of being mere mindless momentum?

feedback.correct_en: 「惰性」 (dasei) literally 'inertia' — doing something only because that's how it's always been. It's exactly the critical label Mai throws back at Souma.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「伝統」 'tradition' is positive/neutral and wouldn't be dismissive, and 「情熱」 'passion' is the opposite of what she's accusing him of.

contrast_examples.jp: 惰性で続けているだけだ。
contrast_examples.en: We're only continuing out of inertia.

contrast_examples.jp: 長い伝統を守る。
contrast_examples.en: We preserve a long tradition.

prompt.context_jp: 舞に押し切られた相馬が落胆する場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 副支店長は、大きなため息とともに肩を___しかなかった。
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb completes this body-language collocation of disappointment?

feedback.correct_en: 「肩を落とす」 is the set phrase for slumping one's shoulders in disappointment or resignation. It pairs naturally with 「ため息」.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「肩を上げる」 isn't idiomatic for emotion, and 「肩を振る」 isn't a standard expression for this feeling at all.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は肩を落として帰っていった。
contrast_examples.en: He went home with slumped shoulders.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は肩をすくめた。
contrast_examples.en: He shrugged his shoulders.

prompt.context_jp: 優秀な女子行員が来ると聞いた相馬の反応。
prompt.prompt_jp: 優秀な若い女子行員が来ると聞き、相馬は素直に胸を___。
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb completes this idiom of relief?

feedback.correct_en: 「胸を撫でおろす」 = to breathe a sigh of relief after a worry passes. Perfect for Souma, who feared another Mai-type subordinate.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「胸を張る」 means 'to be proud,' and 「胸を痛める」 means 'to be heartbroken' — opposite emotional directions.

contrast_examples.jp: 無事と聞いて胸を撫でおろした。
contrast_examples.en: I was relieved to hear they were safe.

contrast_examples.jp: 成果に胸を張る。
contrast_examples.en: To be proud of one's results.

prompt.context_jp: 本部異動が決まり、相馬が思わず――
prompt.prompt_jp: 口元が___のを抑えられない。
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb describes a face involuntarily breaking into a smile?

feedback.correct_en: 「口元が緩む」 is the standard way to say one's mouth relaxes into a smile against one's will — exactly Souma's inner glee.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「固まる」 (freeze/stiffen) is the opposite reaction, and 「震える」 (tremble) usually signals fear or anger, not satisfied relief.

contrast_examples.jp: 思わず口元が緩む。
contrast_examples.en: A smile unintentionally plays on one's lips.

contrast_examples.jp: 驚きで表情が固まった。
contrast_examples.en: His expression froze in surprise.

prompt.context_jp: 相馬が舞に「余計なことを言わないコツ」を授ける。
prompt.prompt_jp: 言いたいことがあったら、それを言わずに1回 息を___んだ。
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb goes with 「息を」 here?

feedback.correct_en: 「息を吸う」 = to breathe in. Souma's trick is: before speaking, take one breath and swallow the words with it.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「息を切る」 means 'to be out of breath,' and 「息を飲む」 is 'to gasp (in awe/shock)' — neither matches a deliberate pause-and-think breath.

contrast_examples.jp: 深く息を吸ってから話す。
contrast_examples.en: Take a deep breath before speaking.

contrast_examples.jp: 美しさに息をのむ。
contrast_examples.en: To be breathtaken by beauty.

prompt.context_jp: 上司に反論する前に、舞が繰り返し使う前置き。
prompt.prompt_jp: お言葉を___ようですが、女子行員はコストですか？
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb completes this polite but pointed 'with respect, but…' opener?

feedback.correct_en: 「お言葉を返すようですが」 is a set phrase meaning 'I don't mean to talk back, but…' — a polite shield for disagreement. Mai uses it twice in this chapter.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「伝える」 would mean 'convey,' and 「預かる」 'take charge of' — neither forms the fixed expression.

contrast_examples.jp: お言葉を返すようですが、賛成できません。
contrast_examples.en: With respect, I can't agree.

contrast_examples.jp: お言葉ですが、少し違います。
contrast_examples.en: If I may say so, it's a bit different.

prompt.context_jp: 相馬が辛島に舞の性格を説明する。
prompt.prompt_jp: 怖いもの知らずで、一度 ___が入ると、上司相手でも止まらなくなる。
prompt.prompt_en: Which word completes this idiom for Mai 'getting fired up'?

feedback.correct_en: 「スイッチが入る」 is the common idiom for 'to switch on / go into unstoppable mode' when someone's temper or drive kicks in. It's Souma's recurring word for Mai.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「エンジンがかかる」 exists but means 'to get warmed up' and uses かかる, not 入る. 「ギアが入る」 is not idiomatic in Japanese in this emotional sense.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女はスイッチが入ると止まらない。
contrast_examples.en: Once she's switched on, she doesn't stop.

contrast_examples.jp: ようやくエンジンがかかってきた。
contrast_examples.en: I'm finally getting into gear.

prompt.context_jp: 追い出しても追い出しても、舞の顔が思い出されてしまう相馬。
prompt.prompt_jp: いくら追い出しても、舞の顔が瞼の裏に___。
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb describes a face vividly resurfacing in the mind's eye?

feedback.correct_en: 「瞼の裏に浮かぶ」 is the standard collocation for an image floating up behind one's closed eyes. 浮かんでくる adds the 'keeps coming up despite himself' nuance.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「沈む」 would mean 'sink' (wrong direction for memories) and 「降りてくる」 (descend) isn't used for mental images.

contrast_examples.jp: 昔の顔が瞼の裏に浮かんでくる。
contrast_examples.en: An old face floats up behind my eyelids.

contrast_examples.jp: 気分が沈む。
contrast_examples.en: My spirits sink.

prompt.context_jp: 舞が相馬に食い下がる場面。原文:「納得できません。課長は私に任せてくださるとおっしゃいましたよね？」
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds most natural for a junior employee pushing back on her boss in this scene?

choices.text: 課長は私に任せてくださるとおっしゃいましたよね？
課長は私に任せてくれると言いましたよね？
課長は俺に任せると言ったよね？

feedback.correct_en: At work, a junior employee quoting her boss uses 尊敬語 like 「おっしゃいました」 and 「くださる」. This matches Mai's register in the actual line.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B drops to plain polite with no respectful verbs — too flat for quoting a 課長. Option C uses casual 俺/言った, which no female teller would use to her boss's face.

contrast_examples.jp: 部長がそうおっしゃいました。
contrast_examples.en: The manager said so (respectful quote).

contrast_examples.jp: 部長がそう言った。
contrast_examples.en: The manager said that (plain, in-group talk).

prompt.context_jp: 相馬が舞に、臨店先での心構えを叩き込む場面。
prompt.prompt_en: Which version best fits Souma warning his subordinate about visiting other branches?

choices.text: 同じ銀行でも、よそさまの会社だと思え。
同じ銀行でも、他の会社と同じだと考えてください。
同じ銀行でも、違う会社みたいなやつらだぞ。

feedback.correct_en: 「よそさま」 adds a sardonic, old-school politeness — 'treat them as if they were an outside firm' — exactly Souma's seasoned, slightly cynical voice to a subordinate.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is grammatical but flat and overly polite for a boss-to-subordinate directive. C is too crude and insulting toward the other branch — not Souma's measured style.

contrast_examples.jp: よそさまの迷惑になる。
contrast_examples.en: You'll be a nuisance to other people (slightly ironic polite).

contrast_examples.jp: 他人の家に入るな。
contrast_examples.en: Don't enter other people's houses (neutral/direct).

prompt.context_jp: 舞が茅場町支店長の矢島に正面から反論する場面。
prompt.prompt_en: Which opener best captures Mai's style — polite surface, sharp content — when she pushes back on the branch manager?

choices.text: お言葉を返すようですが、女子行員はコストですか？
ちょっと言わせてもらいますけど、女子行員ってコストなんですか？
黙れ、女子行員はコストじゃない。

feedback.correct_en: 「お言葉を返すようですが」 is the signature phrase that lets Mai challenge a superior while staying technically polite — it's the chapter's recurring motif.
feedback.incorrect_en: B drops to casual-polite and loses the formal edge that gives her words weight in a 応接室. C is openly rude and would get her fired, not reasoned with.

contrast_examples.jp: お言葉を返すようですが、それは違います。
contrast_examples.en: With respect, that's not right.

contrast_examples.jp: ちょっと言わせて。
contrast_examples.en: Let me say something (casual).

prompt.context_jp: 舞が「たかが窓口」発言に反応しかけた瞬間、相馬が小声で釘を刺す。
prompt.prompt_en: Which line fits Souma hissing at Mai under his breath?

choices.text: 花咲！ スイッチは入れんなよ。
花咲さん、感情的にならないでいただけますか。
花咲、スイッチを入れないようにしてください。

feedback.correct_en: In the moment, Souma uses blunt in-group speech to his subordinate — surname + casual imperative 「入れんなよ」 (= 入れるなよ). It fits the panicked, under-the-table warning.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is office-polite — too formal and slow for a whispered warning while a client is right there. C is grammatical but mixes casual address with ます-form, sounding stilted.

contrast_examples.jp: 騒ぐなよ！
contrast_examples.en: Don't make a fuss! (casual, urgent)

contrast_examples.jp: お静かにお願いします。
contrast_examples.en: Please be quiet. (polite customer-facing)

prompt.context_jp: 舞が相馬を押し切る直前、キャンセル料をちらつかせる。
prompt.prompt_en: Which version matches Mai's playful, pushy delivery as she corners her boss?

choices.text: 今からだとキャンセル料取られちゃうんで、いいですよね？ ねっねっねっ？
今からだとキャンセル料を取られてしまいますので、よろしいでしょうか。
今キャンセルすると金取られる。いいだろ？

feedback.correct_en: The repeated 「ねっねっねっ？」 and 「〜ちゃうんで」 give Mai her trademark half-polite, cheerfully-steamrolling tone — polite ending but zero room for refusal.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is too formal — it strips out the pushy warmth that makes the moment funny. C uses male-coded casual 「だろ？」 and bluntness that doesn't fit her persona or the workplace.

contrast_examples.jp: もう予約しちゃったんで、いいですよね？
contrast_examples.en: I already booked it — that's fine, right? (coaxing)

contrast_examples.jp: すでに予約済みですので、ご了承ください。
contrast_examples.en: I have already booked it; please understand. (formal)
